summary: Defines an experimental MIB module with managed objects for monitoring Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) devices, covering basic configuration, functional status and operational counters and statistics. It is useful to operators who want to watch such devices with SNMP-style management tools.

eli5.summary: A dashboard where network managers can read the dials of special routers.

questions: how to monitor lisp devices with snmp
how do i monitor lisp routers with snmp
how do lisp device roles show up in snmp
subtitle: A dashboard for operators to monitor LISP routers and networks with SNMP tools.

tldr.problem: Networks that use LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) need a way to monitor and manage these specialized routers from a central point. Standard SNMP monitoring tools do not understand LISP's unique configuration and statistics.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7052 defines a LISP MIB module, a set of read-only data objects that SNMP tools can query to report on LISP device status, configuration, cache contents, and traffic statistics.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now use standard SNMP-based management platforms to see what is happening inside LISP networks without building custom monitoring code.

facts.label: Main tables
facts.value: 12 (features, statistics, mapping database, map cache, registration, Map-Server/Resolver state)

facts.label: Compliance profiles
facts.value: 6 (one for each LISP role: ITR, ETR, PITR, PETR, Map-Server, Map-Resolver)

today: RFC 7052 is an Experimental specification. It is in use in LISP implementations and test networks as the standard way to expose LISP device state to SNMP management tools. The MIB has not been superseded or made obsolete; it remains the sole RFC-standard management interface for LISP devices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7052 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). A MIB is a structured set of managed objects—variables and counters—that network devices expose so that operators and automated tools can monitor and learn about their state.

The LISP MIB is specifically designed for devices that run the Locator/ID Separation Protocol, a network architecture that separates IP addresses into two roles: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) used within sites, and Routing Locators (RLOCs) used on the Internet backbone. This separation allows networks to scale and change addresses without disrupting the Internet's routing table.

By implementing this MIB, a LISP device allows operators to query its configuration, feature status, cache contents, and statistics using standard SNMP tools. All objects in this MIB are read-only, so no remote SNMP client can change device state through the MIB—monitoring only, no control.
sections.eli5: This RFC is a menu of dials that LISP routers expose. You can ask the router questions like 'How many messages came in?' or 'What is your cache size?' and it will answer. You cannot tell it to do anything—just look.

sections.title: LISP Device Roles and Features
sections.content:
The MIB recognizes six different LISP roles that a single device can take on. An Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) is where packets enter the LISP network; it encapsulates them and sends them to Egress Tunnel Routers (ETRs), which decapsulate them and deliver them to their destination sites. A Proxy ITR (PITR) lets non-LISP sites send traffic into a LISP network, and a Proxy ETR (PETR) lets LISP sites reach non-LISP destinations. A Map-Server holds a database of EID-to-RLOC mappings that ETRs register with; a Map-Resolver answers queries about where to find a given EID.

For each Instance ID (a number that partitions traffic into virtual networks) and address family (IPv4, IPv6, or LCAF—LISP Canonical Address Format), the MIB tracks whether each role is enabled on the device. It also monitors related tunables such as the size limit of the ITR's map-cache (the on-demand cache that remembers where EIDs are located) and the TTL of cached entries.
sections.eli5: LISP routers wear different hats: some wrap up packages and send them down the tube (ITR), some unwrap them at the other end (ETR), and some keep directories of who is where (Map-Server). The MIB shows which hats each router is wearing and lets you tweak how well it remembers things.

sections.title: MIB Tables and Managed Objects
sections.content:
The LISP MIB module is organized into twelve main tables. The lispFeaturesTable reports which LISP roles are active and holds configuration limits. The lispMappingDatabase and lispMapCache tables expose the two main data stores: the ETR's static database of the prefixes it serves and the ITR's dynamic cache of where it recently learned EIDs live. Parallel locator tables break down the RLOCs within each mapping.

For ETRs operating as Map-Servers, the lispEidRegistration tables track which EIDs are registered by which ETRs, the timestamps of registration messages, authentication errors, and locator mismatches. For ITRs using Map-Resolvers, a table records the state of configured Map-Resolvers and Proxy ETRs. A lispConfiguredLocator table lists all RLOCs configured on the device.

In all tables, the MIB uses a custom textual convention, LispAddressType, to represent addresses of multiple families (IPv4, IPv6, LCAF) in a uniform four-tuple: address family number, address length, the address bytes, and a prefix mask length.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like several file cabinets. One has cards for each role and what it is doing. Another has pages for each network it knows about and where to find it. A third keeps notes about every router that registered with it. The custom address format is a clever way to say '2001:db8::1/64' without fixing the size.

sections.title: Counters and Diagnostics
sections.content:
The MIB tracks several classes of counters for network operations. The lispGlobalStatsTable counts control-plane messages: map-requests in and out, map-replies in and out, and map-registers in and out. These counters help operators spot control-plane problems or load patterns. At a finer grain, the mapping and cache tables count encapsulated and decapsulated octets and packets for each EID-Prefix or RLOC, allowing an operator to see traffic patterns on a per-prefix basis.

For devices acting as Map-Servers, there are counters for authentication errors and RLOC mismatches in registration messages—red flags that suggest misconfiguration or attack. Each entry also records timestamps of configuration changes and last activity, so an operator can diagnose staleness or performance issues.

All counters are read-only, and SNMP rules state that if a counter wraps or the device reboots, the timestamp shows when that happened, so monitoring systems can detect discontinuities.
sections.eli5: Like a cash register tape, the MIB keeps a tally of every message sent and every packet wrapped or unwrapped. It also notes when something went wrong—like a registration that failed because the password did not match. From these tallies, a manager can spot problems or bottlenecks.

sections.title: Compliance and Deployment
sections.content:
The MIB defines six compliance profiles—one for each major LISP role: ETR, ITR, Proxy-ITR, Proxy-ETR, Map-Server, and Map-Resolver. A device declares which profile it supports, describing which object groups are mandatory for that role and which are optional. A basic ITR, for instance, must support the ITR group (core ITR objects) but may optionally report ITR extended diagnostics, Map-Server role objects, or statistics groups.

When a network operator deploys this MIB on a LISP device, they configure SNMPv3 with user authentication and privacy (the RFC strongly recommends against older SNMP versions, which have weak security). The operator can then query or poll the device using SNMP tools or collectors, building dashboards in systems like Nagios, Grafana, or vendor-supplied management platforms. The read-only nature of the MIB means that misconfiguration via SNMP is not possible; the device's command-line interface remains the source of truth for changes.
sections.eli5: The MIB says 'if you are an ITR, you must show these dials; if you also do Map-Server work, show these extras if you can.' A manager hooks the router up to a monitoring system using a secure protocol and starts watching. The dials are all read-only, so the monitor can never accidentally break the router.
